title: Subscriber Notification Delivery Flow
purpose: Show how new content notifications are delivered to subscribers with fire-and-forget semantics, highlighting the absence of real-time delivery
audience: Backend developers, content workflow engineers, notification system maintainers
description: When a creator publishes new content, the content service triggers NotificationService.notifySubscribersOfNewContent() as a fire-and-forget operation via .catch(). The notification service fetches all active subscriptions for the creator, then iterates each subscriber to check their preferences.notifications.newContent flag. For opted-in subscribers, a notification record is created in the notifications table. The entire method is fire-and-forget: errors are silently swallowed by .catch(). Notifications are NOT pushed via Socket.IO — subscribers only see them on their next page load via REST GET /api/v1/notifications.

validationRules: Notification type must be 'new_content' for this flow
Creator must have completed content creation (valid content record)
Subscription must have status = 'active' to be included
Preferences.notifications.newContent defaults to true if field is missing
businessRules: Fire-and-forget via .catch() — entire notification method has no delivery guarantee
No Socket.IO push — notifications are passive; subscriber must poll REST endpoint
Per-notification failure isolation is good — one subscriber failure does not cascade
No batch insert optimization — each subscriber gets individual insert
No retry on failure — best-effort delivery only
Scheduled (future-publish) content does NOT trigger notifications at publish time
securityConsiderations: Notification delivery is purely server-side — no user data leaked via client interaction
Subscriber preferences are respected — opt-out honored
Error details may include PII in console.error logs (user IDs, etc.)
No notification content includes sensitive data beyond content title and creator username
performanceConsiderations: Each subscriber gets individual DB insert — scales linearly with subscriber count
No batching — for creators with many subscribers, this creates many individual transactions
Fire-and-forget does not block the content creation response — good for UX
No background job queue — all processing happens in the same Node.js event loop tick (unawaited promise)
Could cause memory pressure if subscriber list is very large and notifications fail before all are created
